description: Beam span divided by beam depth
source: Rule of thumb span/depth ~20 for glulam beams (civilsir.com/glulam-span-rule-of-thumb)
comments: Single, US-origin rule of thumb; kept range 16-24. Worth checking against EN 1995 / Dutch practice (span/depth 15-20).

description: Beam depth divided by beam width
source: Beam width = 1/3 to 1/4 of depth (civilsir.com/glulam-span-rule-of-thumb); APA limits depth/width to <=12 (anthonyforest.com APA TT-085)
comments: Typical moved from 3 to 3.5 (midpoint of the 3-4 rule of thumb). Lowers beam mass ~14% vs before.

source: common sense: between EN 14080 GL24h (~420) and Annebergs EPD (461)
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): GL24h spruce glulam has a mean density of ~420 kg/m3 (EN 14080, from memory) and the Danish EPD declares 461, so 439 sits between the two. Fixed because timber is bought per m3. | earlier note: fixed: glulam timber is bought in m3, at 1 / density m3 per kg of product (production row). 461 (EPD) vs 439 is a 5% difference; if you change this, change the production row to 1/density too. | [2026-10-16] Range 351.2-526.8 -> 419-459: GL24h glulam ~420 kg/m3, Danish EPD 461 kg/m3

description: Amount of glulam timber per kg of product
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): Exactly 1/density: 1 kg of beam needs 1/439 m3 of glulam, no cutting waste modelled (offcuts are inside the cradle-to-gate dataset). | earlier note: 1 / 439 kg per m3 | [2026-10-16] Fixed (was a +-20 % range): exactly 1 / density

description: Years the product lasts in use
source: Assumed equal to the reinforced concrete beam (structural frame element, protected interior). EN 1990 design working life 50 y (class 3) to 100 y (class 4) (betonhuis.nl); Annebergs glulam EPD declares no RSL
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): A protected glulam beam does not rot or fatigue, so it lasts as long as the building it sits in. Used the same 75 y as concrete (range 50-100 y) so the comparison is not tilted by lifetime alone. | earlier note: Raised from 60. No glulam-specific reference service life found; equal lifetimes avoid biasing the comparison (burdens are scaled by service_life / L). Decision for you: keep 75 or set a glulam-specific value.

description: kg of glulam timber that goes to waste incineration at end of life, per kg of product
source: common sense, cross-checked with Annebergs glulam EPD (47% recycling / 53% incineration / 0% landfill)
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): Kept your numbers (you said they look fine). Reasoning: glue and preservatives make post-consumer glulam grade B/C wood, which goes mostly to energy recovery (Danish EPD: 53% energy, 47% chips) with a smaller part to chipboard; landfilling is banned or rare in NL/DK/DE, so 10% landfill is on the high side and could be ~0-5%.

description: kg of glulam timber that goes to waste recycling at end of life, per kg of product
source: common sense, cross-checked with Annebergs glulam EPD (47% recycling / 53% incineration / 0% landfill)
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): Kept. Recycled into chipboard (open loop); 30% is between practice for glued wood (~10-20%) and the Danish EPD's 47%.

description: kg of glulam timber that goes to waste landfilling at end of life, per kg of product
source: common sense, cross-checked with Annebergs glulam EPD (47% recycling / 53% incineration / 0% landfill)
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): Kept. Probably a slight overestimate for NL (landfill of wood is banned), a reasonable Europe-wide value.

description: Country whose electricity mix is displaced by energy recovered at end of life
comments: Common-sense estimate (Claude, for LCA-team review): Model choice, not a measurement: NL because the RAW project and its electricity/heat credit assumptions are Dutch and the ecoinvent NL grid is available. Only matters for the energy credit of incineration; change on study_setup if you model another country.
